claims.text: Adding approximately 1–3 wt% Ni to a W–Cu precursor blend before sintering will produce a transient Ni-rich liquid phase at W/Cu interfaces.
The Ni-rich interfacial phase will improve wetting and interfacial contact between W and Cu.
Improved W/Cu wetting and contact will reduce void formation and phase separation.
Reduced void formation and phase separation will enhance thermal transport.
The Ni intervention will preserve the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
Conventionally processed W particles or connected W regions in a Cu matrix typically exhibit voids and phase separation.
Ni melts at processing temperatures above 950 °C and can therefore form the proposed liquid phase in the stated 950–1200 °C window.
Keeping the sintering temperature below the boiling point of Cu will avoid degradation of both W and Cu.
The transient Ni-rich phase will enhance capillary wetting, improve interparticle contact, and accelerate mass transfer.
Molten Ni will form a wetting layer at W/Cu boundaries that fills gaps and reduces residual porosity.
Ni at the interfaces will facilitate interfacial diffusion.
Stable intermetallic phases may form during cooling of the Ni-doped W–Cu composite.
Interfacial diffusion and possible intermetallic formation will bond W and Cu more effectively without compromising the integrity of either phase.
Relative to otherwise identical Ni-free SPS W–Cu composites, Ni-doped composites will have lower void content.
Relative to Ni-free SPS W–Cu composites, Ni-doped composites will have a more uniform interpenetrating microstructure.
Relative to Ni-free SPS W–Cu composites, Ni-doped composites will have enhanced thermal conductivity.
The mechanical properties of Ni-doped W–Cu composites will be at least as robust as those obtained by current SPS or vapor-coating methods.
The proposed behavior will remain applicable under high-heat, irradiation-exposed service conditions relevant to fusion-reactor joints.
